title: Permutation in String
description: Brute force to optimized: rebuilding letter counts per window versus an incrementally-maintained sliding window count array.

blocks.text: Given two strings s1 and s2, return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1 as a substring (that is, some contiguous substring of s2 uses exactly the same letters, in any order, as s1).

blocks.caption: Slide a window the size of s1 through s2, comparing letter counts at each position

blocks.text: Given two strings s1 and s2, determine whether s2 contains any substring that is a permutation of s1, meaning it uses the exact same letters, the same number of times each, just possibly in a different order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Searching for an Anagram Hidden in a Longer Text
blocks.text: Like sliding a same-size viewing window through a long passage of text, checking at each position whether the letters visible through the window are exactly a rearrangement of a target word, regardless of their order.

blocks.caption: Slide a same-size window through the text, checking for matching letter counts at each position

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The substring \"ba\" (indices 3-4 of s2)","a permutation of \"ab\"","It uses exactly one a and one b, just in reverse order"],["Answer","true","A qualifying substring was found"]]}

blocks.text: No two-character substring of s2 uses exactly one a and one b together; the a and b in s2 are never adjacent, so no permutation of s1 appears, giving an answer of false.
Edge case: s1 is longer than s2
If s1 is longer than s2, no substring of s2 could ever be long enough to be a permutation of s1, so the answer is immediately false.

Before generating every permutation of s1 (which grows factorially with its length) or rebuilding letter counts for every window from scratch, notice that "is a permutation" is really just "has identical letter counts".

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Two strings of the same length are permutations of each other exactly when they have identical counts of every letter, regardless of order.

Observation 2: This means checking for a permutation of s1 inside s2 reduces to checking every substring of s2 with length equal to s1 for matching letter counts, a fixed-size sliding window problem.

Observation 3: Maintain a running count of letters in the current window, updated the same way any fixed-size window updates: add the entering character, remove the leaving character once the window exceeds size len(s1).

Observation 4: At every fully-formed window, compare its letter-count array directly against s1's own letter-count array; if they match exactly, a permutation has been found.

Reframing "is this a permutation" as "do these two count arrays match" turns an otherwise combinatorial-looking problem into a straightforward fixed-size sliding window comparison.
This "compare letter-count arrays instead of generating actual permutations" reframing is the single most important idea here.
For every possible window of s2 with length equal to s1, build its letter counts from scratch and compare them directly against s1's own letter counts.

items: Precompute the letter counts of s1 once.
For every possible starting position in s2, build the letter counts of that window directly, and compare it against s1's counts.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: need is computed exactly once, outside the main loop, since s1 itself never changes.
A fresh window count is built for every starting position, since each window's letters need to be counted independently.
The function returns true the moment a match is found, without needing to check any remaining windows.

blocks.text: Every window's true letter counts are computed directly, so a matching permutation, if one exists, is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m), where n is the length of s2 and m is the length of s1, since each of the roughly n windows rebuilds its counts from m characters.
Space: O(1) extra, since only 26 possible letters are ever tracked.
Limitation: rebuilding letter counts from scratch for every one of the roughly n windows repeats almost all of the same counting across neighboring windows, since they share m-1 characters.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds the entire window's letter counts from scratch for every position, discarding almost all of that work between neighboring windows that share m-1 characters. Instead, maintain a running letter-count array for the window, updated incrementally as it slides: add the entering character's count, remove the leaving character's count. Compare this running count array against s1's own count array at every fully-formed window, turning each comparison into a fixed 26-length array check instead of an O(m) rebuild.

Precompute s1's letter counts once. Slide a window of length equal to s1 across s2, maintaining its letter counts incrementally. At every fully-formed window, compare its counts directly against s1's counts; a match means a permutation has been found.
Maintain the window's letter counts incrementally, comparing them against s1's counts at every fully-formed window.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass, since each character of s2 is added and removed from the window at most once.
Space: O(1) extra, since only 26 possible letters are ever tracked.

Two strings of the same length are permutations of each other precisely when their letter-count arrays are identical, regardless of the order the letters appear in. Maintaining the window's letter counts incrementally, the same way any fixed-size sliding window updates, means every fully-formed window's count array is always accurate, and comparing it directly to s1's own fixed count array correctly detects a permutation the instant one appears.

items: need is built once from s1, before the main loop, and never changes.
window is updated every time the sliding window moves: incrementing the entering character's count, decrementing the leaving character's count once the window exceeds its target size.
The comparison between window and need only happens once the window has reached its full size, guarded by the index check.

blocks.text: The key reframing, "checking for a permutation is the same as comparing letter-count arrays", turns what looks like a combinatorial problem into a standard fixed-size sliding window comparison.

items: Trying to actually generate or check every permutation of s1 directly, which grows factorially and is far too slow.
Rebuilding the window's letter counts from scratch on every slide instead of updating them incrementally.
Forgetting the early-exit check for when s1 is longer than s2, which can never have a match.

items: State the "permutation equals matching letter counts" reframing explicitly and early, since it is the entire insight needed to solve this efficiently.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Does one string contain a rearrangement (anagram/permutation) of another as a substring" points toward comparing fixed-size sliding window letter counts, not generating actual permutations.

items: How would you find ALL starting indices where a permutation of s1 occurs in s2, not just whether one exists? Continue the sliding window past the first match, collecting every qualifying starting index instead of returning immediately.

What if the alphabet were much larger than 26 letters, such as full Unicode? A hash map instead of a fixed-size array would be needed to track counts, though the sliding window logic itself stays the same.

How would you adapt this to check for a permutation match allowing up to some number of mismatched letters? This becomes more like Longest Repeating Character Replacement, tracking a tolerance for mismatched counts instead of requiring an exact match.
Directly reuses the fixed-size sliding window technique from Maximum Average Subarray I, comparing letter-count arrays instead of tracking a sum.
The same "compare frequency arrays for an exact anagram match" idea reappears in Find All Anagrams in a String, which finds every matching window instead of just the first one.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * m) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (incremental sliding window counts): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window, comparing letter-count arrays instead of generating permutations
Core Idea: Two same-length strings are permutations of each other exactly when their letter counts match exactly
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: "Is a permutation" reframes directly into "has an identical letter-count array", avoiding any combinatorial generation
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Slide the window, compare letter counts, not the letters themselves
